Its own text says SUPERSEDED 2026-08-17 by that rule, and the key has since been renamed (chg:the-key-is-renamed-and-the-sweep-says-what-it-swept); only the status was never moved. properties.decision:
⛔ SUPERSEDED 2026-08-17, HOURS AFTER IT WAS WRITTEN, by `rule:fix-it-properly-while-it-is-still-cheap`. The original text is in `snap:epoch:the-key-is-renamed-and-the-sweep-says-what-it-swept:dec:a-misnaming-is-fixed-in-the-message-not-the-key`, and its reasoning is still the right shape for a project that HAS made a stability commitment — this one has not.

WHAT IT DECIDED, AND WHAT CHANGED. It declined to rename the `disconnected_community` defect category, on the ground that the key is a consumer contract in three places (a documented HEAL category, what `detect_defects` callers match on, and a named ility source) and renaming it would break every consumer to fix a sentence. Anthony's rule reversed exactly that ground: before 1.0 the price of a break is at its lowest and rises with every user, so "it would break consumers" argues for doing it NOW. THE CATEGORY IS NOW `unthreaded_cluster`, which names what is actually missing — a traceability edge, the golden thread — and cannot be misread as "unreachable in the graph".

⭐ AND THE COST ESTIMATE THIS DECISION RESTED ON WAS NEVER CHECKED, which is the part worth carrying forward. It said renaming would "break every consumer" without measuring what that meant. Measured before the rename: the key appears in 14 source and test files and 6 live docs, and 41 times in the committed export — ALL OF THEM PROSE. It was NEVER PERSISTED AS DATA: no node property anywhere holds it as a value, so no observation, no acknowledgement and no ility reading needed migrating. The rename was a sed and a doc pass. A cost asserted rather than measured decided the original call, in a project whose own standing rule is that claims in the records must be evidence-backed.

THE SECOND HALF WAS TAKEN TOO. This decision deferred giving unscoped `detect_defects` the envelope its scoped sibling already returns, as a consumer break out of scope for finishing (b) and (c). Also done: it now returns `{swept, defects}`, so an empty answer says whether it was exercised and found nothing or had nothing to examine.

WHAT SURVIVES UNCHANGED, and it is the load-bearing half. "Make it compute what it claims" is still the wrong fix, for a reason that has nothing to do with cost: the computation is not broken. It runs connected components over `design_network()` correctly, and the narrowness is the deliberate exclusion of provenance types and CONTAINS — each with its own record (BL-84, BL-124). Widening the walk would undo those and report every Fragment as an island. The requirement's own text misdescribes the detector as computing modularity, which it does not. So the third option was right about the ALGORITHM and wrong about the NAME.

📌 THE GENERAL LESSON, sharpened by being wrong: when a name overstates a computation, ask which of the three is actually wrong — the algorithm, the name, or the message — and do not let the cost of fixing one decide the answer before that cost has been measured.

📝 HOW THIS NODE'S OWN HISTORY WAS NEARLY LOST, recorded because it is `req:a-write-cannot-silently-lose-someone-elses-work` happening to the agent writing about it. The supersession was first written by calling `add_decision` on the existing id, which REPLACED three properties. The reply's `revision` block said so and warned that the prior values existed nowhere else — the mitigation that requirement describes as "detection rather than prevention", working exactly as documented. The fix was to restore the original text, `record_change` to snapshot it, and only then apply this one. The lesson is the ordering: record_change BEFORE the merge, never after, or the snapshot captures the replacement and the history is confidently wrong.
properties.name: SUPERSEDED — the message was fixed and the key was not; the key has since been renamed too
properties.rationale: Superseded by rule:fix-it-properly-while-it-is-still-cheap. Its cost argument — that renaming would break every consumer — was asserted and never measured; the key turned out never to have been persisted as data, so the rename needed no migration at all. The algorithm half of its reasoning stands unchanged: the computation is correct and the narrow walk is deliberate, so "make it compute what it claims" remains the wrong fix.
